name: Asymmetric hair part

lead: An asymmetric hair part places the parting off-centre so the hair falls in a way that balances a face whose two sides differ. The change shows as soon as the hair is styled.

Where hair falls shifts visual weight toward one side of the face, which can offset differences in brows, hairline or cheeks. It is a styling idea; research on facial symmetry covers attractiveness ratings, not hairstyle as camouflage.

paras: People try parts on different sides and at different distances from centre, often with a stylist's input, and combine them with a cut that holds the shape. It is set fresh each time you style your hair.
Risks are minimal; it is a reversible styling choice.

chain: Hair falls to offset uneven sides
angle.text: Parting hair off-centre changes where hair falls, so it offsets differences between the two sides of the face and the whole face reads as more balanced. The change is visible as soon as the hair is styled.

lead: An asymmetric hair part is an off-centre parting chosen so the hair falls in a way that visually balances differences between the two sides of the face. People use it to soften a crooked nose, uneven brows or eyes, or a wider or heavier side of the face, so the face reads as more even from the front.[1]

Stylists describe the general principle as asymmetrical balance: a perfectly symmetrical hairstyle can draw attention to uneven features, so the lopsided element of the style is placed opposite the feature being offset.[1] Applied to partings, this means shifting the part to one side, and sometimes deepening it, rather than splitting the hair down the middle.

Facial symmetry is a well-studied topic. Wikipedia reports that symmetry raises attractiveness ratings for both sexes, that symmetric faces are rated as healthier, and that small directional asymmetries, such as eyes, nose and mouth sitting slightly left of the ear axis, are normal in the population.[2] No published study found has tested hair parting as a way to change perceived asymmetry or attractiveness.
infobox: Visually balance uneven sides of the face[1]
Asymmetric cuts, side parts, side sweeps[1]

paras: Wikipedia describes an asymmetric cut as a haircut without left-right symmetry, where one side is cut differently or left longer, and notes that such styles often combine two separate looks, one per side. An extreme form is the side shave.[1] Hairdressers and cosmetologists call the offsetting effect asymmetrical balance: a symmetrical style can draw attention to asymmetries such as a crooked nose, so an asymmetric cut is often recommended, with the hair's asymmetry running opposite to the feature.[1]

The article also says asymmetric styles that show the ears can make the face look slimmer and are often advised for round faces or wide-set eyes, and that an asymmetric cut can draw attention away from eyeglasses and is often seen as more trendy than a symmetrical one.[1] Applied to partings, this means shifting the part to one side, and sometimes deepening it, rather than splitting the hair down the middle.

Stylists commonly recommend a side or slightly off-centre part for uneven faces, reasoning that a centre part emphasises any difference between the two halves of the face while an off-centre part breaks it up. These are practitioner recommendations rather than tested findings.

Facial symmetry is usually measured as fluctuating asymmetry, random left-right differences in features. Wikipedia summarises studies reporting that symmetry raises attractiveness ratings, with a larger effect for female faces (Rhodes et al., 1998), that symmetric faces are rated healthier (Jones et al., 2001), and that symmetry is linked to perceived skin condition (Jones et al., 2004). Symmetry and averageness appear to contribute independently.[2]

Directional asymmetry, a systematic bias across a population, is the best-known facial example: the offset of eyes, nose and mouth from the ear axis falls from about 2 degrees at birth to about 0.5 degrees in adults.[2] The same article lists caveats, including that mirroring face halves creates unnatural features (a slightly bent nose becomes oversized or undersized), which has led some to question conclusions drawn from mirrored-face studies, and that perceived differences may reflect cultural prejudice.[2] It also notes a finding by Perrett et al. (1999) that symmetrising older faces tends to raise attractiveness while symmetrising young adult faces tends to lower it.[2]

In appearance communities, facial asymmetry is a common concern, and hairstyle is discussed among camouflage options alongside makeup, glasses and grooming. Guidance on parting generally comes from stylists rather than studies, and the idea is usually described as shifting visual weight toward one side so that features read as more balanced from the front.[1]

Hairdressing sources describe asymmetrical balance as a design principle.[1] Studies of facial symmetry measure attractiveness ratings of faces rather than hairstyle effects, and no study found measures whether a part changes how symmetric a face is judged to be.[2]
No studies found. Related research on facial symmetry and attractiveness exists but does not test hair parting.[2]

lore.intro: Off-centre parting is discussed as a free, reversible way to downplay uneven features, with advice drawn mostly from stylist convention.[1]

claims.claim: A centre part exaggerates facial asymmetry, so an off-centre part looks better on uneven faces.
The hair's asymmetry should run opposite to the feature being balanced.
Making the face look more symmetric makes it look more attractive.
